The map, filter, and reduce functions
What map, filter and reduce do in JavaScript, how reduce emulates the other two, and how to write all three with a loop, declaratively and via a trampoline.
Understand what map, filter and reduce do, and learn to implement them yourself: declaratively, imperatively and recursively with a trampoline.
text
The most frequently used functions in functional programming and production code are map, filter, and reduce.
These functions provide powerful capabilities for working with data.
heading
map

The map function returns a new object of the same data type, passing each element through the function it receives as an argument when the type is iterable. If the type is not iterable, the contained data is simply passed through the function.
Let's implement the map function in several different ways.
code
filter

The filter function returns a new object of the same data type, passing each element through a predicate function and keeping only the elements for which the predicate returned true (the type is iterable).

A predicate is a function that returns true or false. It is usually passed as an argument to a higher-order function such as filter: in JavaScript functions are first-class values, so they can be passed around like any other value.
Let's implement the filter function in several different ways.
reduce
The reduce function can return any data type; it takes a function and an accumulator as its arguments.

As arguments, the function takes the accumulator (from the initial value or from subsequent calls) and the current element, passes this data through the function's logic, and returns a new accumulator or applies changes to the current accumulator.
The accumulator (the initial value) can be any value.

With reduce you can emulate any custom behavior, as well as the behavior of map and filter. But it is usually used to collect specific data according to a particular logic from an iterable object type.
map returns a new object of the same data type, passing each element through the given function.
filter returns a new object of the same data type and keeps only the elements for which the predicate returned true.
reduce takes a function and an accumulator and can return any data type; with it you can emulate both map and filter.
Currying and taking the data as the last argument let you use these functions in composition in point-free style, without naming the data.
The recursive versions run through a trampoline and walk the array by index: copying the array on every step would make them O(n²).

The lesson says that reduce can emulate map and filter. Write curried functions mapVia and filterVia that take the data as the last argument and use only reduce inside. Then use pipe to build an onlineNames function from them that returns the names of the users who are online.

reduce can return any data type, an object for example. Write a curried function countBy: its first argument is a function that returns an element's key, its second is an array, and it uses reduce to return an object that shows, for each key, how many elements produced it. Count the users by status, and the numbers from 1 to 5 by parity.
